entities.evidence: The form לְאָדָם lacks the definite article. God addresses Adam as the husband who listened to his wife and ate from the forbidden tree, matching the existing person tag.

review.translation: [Then to Adam|0] [he said|1], “[Because|2] [you listened|3] [to the voice of|4] [your wife|5] [and ate|6] [from|7] [the tree|8] [about which|9] [I commanded you|10], [saying|11], ‘[You must|13] [not|12] [eat|13] [from it|14],’ [the ground|16] [is cursed|15] [because of you|17]. [By painful toil|18] [you will eat|19] {from} [it|19] [all|20] [the days of|21] [your life|22].

analysis.evidence: וּלְאָדָם אָמַר introduces the person God addresses. The pointing לְאָדָם has no definite article, which favors the personal name. God identifies Adam’s action in the words ‘you listened to your wife’s voice and ate from the tree.’
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וּ ‘and’ + preposition לְ ‘to’ + masculine singular proper name אָדָם.

analysis.evidence: וּלְאָדָם identifies Adam as the addressee. אָמַר introduces God's words to him, beginning כִּי שָׁמַעְתָּ, “because you listened.”
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person masculine singular, with no prefix or suffix

analysis.evidence: Within God’s speech to Adam, כִּי introduces the reason for the judgment. Adam listened to his wife (שָׁמַעְתָּ לְקוֹל אִשְׁתֶּךָ) and ate from the tree (וַתֹּאכַל מִן הָעֵץ). The judgment follows in אֲרוּרָה הָאֲדָמָה בַּעֲבוּרֶךָ, “the ground is cursed because of you.”
analysis.morphology: Uninflected causal conjunction without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: לְקוֹל אִשְׁתֶּךָ identifies whose voice Adam heeded. The following וַתֹּאכַל (“and you ate”) shows how he acted on his wife’s words despite the command לֹא תֹאכַל (“you shall not eat”).
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, second person masculine singular, with the ending ־תָּ.

analysis.evidence: שָׁמַעְתָּ לְקוֹל אִשְׁתֶּךָ means “you heeded your wife.” The following וַתֹּאכַל, “and you ate,” identifies the action Adam took in response to her words.
analysis.morphology: Prefixed preposition לְ + common noun, masculine singular construct, followed by אִשְׁתֶּךָ.

analysis.evidence: God tells Adam, שָׁמַעְתָּ לְקוֹל אִשְׁתֶּךָ, “you listened to the voice of your wife.” The suffix identifies Adam as the husband.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular common noun in the construct state with a second-person masculine singular possessive suffix.

analysis.evidence: וַתֹּאכַל continues שָׁמַעְתָּ (“you listened”) with Adam still addressed as “you.” The phrase מִן הָעֵץ (“from the tree”) identifies what he ate from, echoing the command לֹא תֹאכַל מִמֶּנּוּ (“you shall not eat from it”).
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, second person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־.

draft.change: Add Genesis 3:17 to the evidence for the Hebrew source sense in the existing min article.
draft.definition: מִן marks the source from which something is taken. With אָכַל here it identifies the tree from which the food comes.
draft.evidence: In Genesis 3:17, מִמֶּנּוּ in the prohibition refers back to מִן הָעֵץ in the account of Adam’s eating.

analysis.evidence: In Genesis 3:17, וַתֹּאכַל מִן הָעֵץ means “you ate from the tree.” The tree is the source of the fruit Adam ate. The quoted command לֹא תֹאכַל מִמֶּנּוּ, “you shall not eat from it,” repeats the construction and refers to the same tree.
analysis.morphology: Independent preposition without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: וַתֹּאכַל מִן הָעֵץ means “you ate from the tree.” The prohibition לֹא תֹאכַל מִמֶּנּוּ (“you shall not eat from it”) identifies the particular tree.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הָ־ prefixed to a masculine singular absolute noun.

analysis.evidence: אֲשֶׁר introduces a relative clause modifying הָעֵץ, “the tree.” The suffix in מִמֶּנּוּ, “from it,” refers back to the tree within the quoted command לֹא תֹאכַל מִמֶּנּוּ, “you shall not eat from it.”
analysis.morphology: Uninflected relative particle

analysis.evidence: God addresses Adam. The suffix ־ךָ identifies Adam as the recipient, and לֵאמֹר introduces the command itself, לֹא תֹאכַל מִמֶּנּוּ (“You shall not eat from it”).
analysis.morphology: Piel perfect, first person common singular, with a second person masculine singular object suffix

analysis.evidence: After צִוִּיתִיךָ (“I commanded you”), לֵאמֹר introduces the words of the command, לֹא תֹאכַל מִמֶּנּוּ (“You shall not eat from it”).
analysis.morphology: Qal infinitive construct with prefixed preposition לְ, realized as לֵ־

analysis.evidence: צִוִּיתִיךָ לֵאמֹר (“I commanded you, saying”) introduces the quoted command לֹא תֹאכַל מִמֶּנּוּ (“you shall not eat from it”). לֹא negates the second-person masculine singular imperfect תֹאכַל, prohibiting Adam from eating from the tree.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected Hebrew negative particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: God quotes his command to Adam, לֹא תֹאכַל מִמֶּנּוּ, “you shall not eat from it.” The separate לֹא supplies the negation, and מִמֶּנּוּ refers to the tree.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, second person masculine singular

draft.change: Add Genesis 3:17 to the evidence for the Hebrew source sense in the existing min article.
draft.definition: מִן marks the source from which something is taken. With אָכַל here it identifies the tree from which the food comes.
draft.evidence: In Genesis 3:17, מִמֶּנּוּ in the prohibition refers back to מִן הָעֵץ in the account of Adam’s eating.

analysis.evidence: וַתֹּאכַל מִן הָעֵץ says that Adam ate from the tree. The quoted command לֹא תֹאכַל מִמֶּנּוּ repeats the same verb and preposition. The suffix resumes הָעֵץ, the masculine singular noun for the tree that supplied the food. This antecedent resolves the suffix as ‘it’ despite the identical form for ‘from us’.
analysis.morphology: Preposition with a third-person masculine singular pronominal suffix referring to הָעֵץ.

draft.change: Broaden the proposed Qal definition to include a curse pronounced on a thing, and cite the feminine participle applied to the ground.
draft.definition: To pronounce a curse on someone or something. The passive participle describes whoever or whatever is under the curse.
draft.evidence: In Gen.3.17 Yahweh addresses Adam, but the subject of אֲרוּרָה is הָאֲדָמָה, the ground. In Gen.3.14 the corresponding masculine form אָרוּר describes the serpent.

analysis.evidence: In אֲרוּרָה הָאֲדָמָה, “cursed is the ground,” the feminine singular participle agrees with הָאֲדָמָה. Yahweh declares the ground cursed on Adam’s account and tells him that he will eat from it in toil all his life.
analysis.morphology: Qal passive participle, feminine singular absolute, used predicatively.
analysis.sense: To pronounce a curse on someone or something.

analysis.evidence: אֲרוּרָה agrees with הָאֲדָמָה in gender and number, yielding “cursed is the ground.” The feminine singular suffix in תֹּאכֲלֶנָּה refers back to the ground, from which the man will obtain food through toil.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular absolute noun with the prefixed definite article הָ־.
analysis.sense: the ground that is tilled; soil

analysis.evidence: In אֲרוּרָה הָאֲדָמָה בַּעֲבוּרֶךָ, the suffix refers to Adam. The preceding כִּי clause identifies his eating from the forbidden tree as the reason the ground is cursed, giving בַּעֲבוּרֶךָ its causal sense.
analysis.morphology: Preposition בְּ־, realized as בַּ־ before עֲ, + masculine singular construct עֲבוּר + second-person masculine singular suffix ־ֶךָ.
analysis.sense: for the sake of, on account of, because of

analysis.evidence: After the ground is cursed, בְּעִצָּבוֹן modifies תֹּאכֲלֶנָּה and describes the toil with which Adam will obtain food from the ground all his life.
analysis.morphology: Preposition בְּ marking manner + masculine singular absolute noun עִצָּבוֹן.

analysis.evidence: The verb addresses Adam. Its feminine singular suffix refers to הָאֲדָמָה, “the ground.” What Adam will eat is what the ground yields. בְּעִצָּבוֹן describes the toil this will cost him.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, second masculine singular, with a third feminine singular object suffix.

analysis.evidence: In כֹּל יְמֵי חַיֶּיךָ, “all the days of your life,” כֹּל takes the plural phrase יְמֵי חַיֶּיךָ as its complement. The phrase gives the duration of Adam’s toil, extending it over his whole life.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular construct noun

analysis.evidence: In כֹּל יְמֵי חַיֶּיךָ, “all the days of your life,” יְמֵי is in construct with חַיֶּיךָ, “your life.” The phrase says how long Adam will eat in toil.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural construct noun
analysis.sense: (pl.) days of a life, a reign or an age

analysis.evidence: כֹּל יְמֵי חַיֶּיךָ means “all the days of your life.” The suffix refers to Adam, and the phrase specifies how long he will eat from the ground in toil.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural noun in the construct state with a second-person masculine singular possessive suffix ־ךָ.
analysis.sense: lifetime, the days of one's life
